questions.stem: A 4-year-old who has not had all recommended vaccines is brought in with a fever of 39.8 °C (103.6 °F) that started 4 hours ago. The child is drooling, sits leaning forward with the neck extended, has muffled speech and is anxious. The SpO2 is 93%. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep the child on the parent's lap and ready the airway equipment
Look at the throat with a tongue blade and a penlight
Lay the child flat to obtain a lateral neck x-ray
Swab the throat for a rapid strep test before starting antibiotics

rationale.correct: Epiglottitis: drooling, dysphagia, distress and tripod position; nothing in the mouth and airway equipment ready.

perOption.a: This suggests epiglottitis; keeping the child calm and upright and having airway equipment ready prevents complete obstruction.
perOption.b: Examining the throat can trigger laryngospasm and complete obstruction.
perOption.c: The child keeps the position of comfort; lying flat can close the airway.
perOption.d: Nothing is placed in the mouth until the airway is secured.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old is brought to the emergency department with a breathing problem. The nurse suspects epiglottitis rather than croup. Select the 3 findings most consistent with epiglottitis.

options.text: Drooling and refusing to swallow saliva
High fever that began a few hours ago
Sitting upright and leaning forward on the hands
A barking, seal-like cough that is worse at night
Symptoms that began with a cold 3 days ago
A hoarse voice with a low-grade fever

rationale.correct: Epiglottitis: the 3 D's (drooling, dysphagia, distress), sudden high fever and tripod position.

perOption.a: Painful swallowing leads to drooling.
perOption.b: Epiglottitis is a rapidly progressing bacterial infection.
perOption.c: The tripod position helps keep the airway open.
perOption.d: This is typical of croup.
perOption.e: Croup follows a viral prodrome; epiglottitis develops over hours.
perOption.f: Hoarseness and a low fever fit viral croup.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Three children are admitted to the pediatric unit with respiratory illnesses. For each finding, indicate which condition it is most consistent with.

rows.text: Barking, seal-like cough that worsens at night
A 3-month-old with wheezing and copious nasal secretions
Toxic appearance with sudden high fever
Inspiratory stridor after 2 days of runny nose
Apnea spells in a 6-week-old born at 33 weeks

rationale.correct: Croup = bark and stridor; epiglottitis = drooling and toxicity; bronchiolitis = infant wheeze with secretions and apnea risk.

perOption.r1:c1: This is the classic croup cough.
perOption.r1:c2: Epiglottitis rarely causes a barking cough.
perOption.r2:c1: Croup does not usually cause drooling.
perOption.r2:c2: Swelling of the epiglottis makes swallowing painful.
perOption.r2:c3: This is not typical of bronchiolitis.
perOption.r3:c3: RSV bronchiolitis causes wheezing and heavy secretions in infants.
perOption.r4:c1: Croup usually has a low-grade fever.
perOption.r4:c2: Epiglottitis is a rapid bacterial infection.
perOption.r4:c3: Bronchiolitis usually has a mild fever.
perOption.r5:c1: Viral croup follows cold symptoms and narrows the subglottic airway.
perOption.r5:c2: Epiglottitis develops over hours without a prodrome.
perOption.r5:c3: Bronchiolitis causes expiratory wheeze, not stridor.
perOption.r6:c1: Croup is rare in young infants.
perOption.r6:c3: Young and premature infants with RSV are at risk for apnea.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with croup has a barking cough, stridor at rest and suprasternal retractions. The SpO2 is 95% and the child is alert. Racemic epinephrine was given by nebulizer 30 minutes ago and the stridor has resolved. The parent asks to go home. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: The child stays 2 to 4 hours to watch for stridor coming back
The child can go home now, since the stridor has fully resolved with treatment
The child needs IV antibiotics before discharge
The child should use a cough suppressant at home tonight

rationale.correct: Croup: dexamethasone for all; racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest, then observe 2 to 4 hours for rebound.

perOption.a: Racemic epinephrine wears off in about 2 hours, and swelling can return (rebound).
perOption.b: The effect may wear off and the stridor can return.
perOption.c: Croup is usually viral.
perOption.d: This does not treat airway swelling.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old with RSV bronchiolitis has thick nasal secretions, a respiratory rate of 58/min, mild retractions and takes only half of each feeding before tiring. The SpO2 is 94% on room air. Which intervention is most helpful?

options.text: Suction the nose with saline before each feeding
Ask the provider for an oral antibiotic
Place the infant flat on the back after feeds
Offer larger feedings less often to reduce tiring

rationale.correct: Bronchiolitis: nasal suctioning, hydration, oxygen if needed and contact precautions.

perOption.a: Infants breathe through the nose; clearing it makes feeding easier.
perOption.b: RSV is viral, and antibiotics do not help.
perOption.c: Raising the head of the crib eases breathing.
perOption.d: Small, frequent feedings use less energy.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with cystic fibrosis has bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools and is below the 10th percentile for weight. The provider prescribes pancrelipase capsules. Which instruction should the nurse give the parent?

options.text: Give the capsules within 30 minutes before each meal and snack
Give the capsules once a day at bedtime on an empty stomach
Crush the capsules and mix them into a cup of warm milk
Give the capsules on the days when the stools look greasy or bulky

rationale.correct: Cystic fibrosis: enzymes with every meal and snack, a high-calorie, high-protein diet and fat-soluble vitamins.

perOption.a: Enzymes must be in the gut with food to digest fat and protein.
perOption.b: There is no food to digest at bedtime.
perOption.c: Crushing and mixing with dairy or hot food destroys the coating.
perOption.d: Enzymes are taken with all meals and snacks.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with cystic fibrosis eats breakfast at 0730, lunch at 1200 and dinner at 1730, and uses albuterol twice daily. The nurse is planning the schedule for chest physiotherapy. Which time is best for the morning session?

options.text: 0700, right after the albuterol and before breakfast
0800, right after breakfast while the child is awake
0700, right before the albuterol is given
1300, after lunch when the child has more energy

rationale.correct: CF airway clearance: daily, before meals or at least 1 hour after, after a bronchodilator.

perOption.a: A bronchodilator first opens the airways, and treatment before meals reduces vomiting.
perOption.b: Treatment after a meal may cause vomiting.
perOption.c: The bronchodilator is given first to open the airways.
perOption.d: Treatment after a meal may cause vomiting.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 8-month-old has had three episodes of pneumonia, frequent large, greasy stools and poor weight gain despite a good appetite. The parent says the baby's skin tastes salty when kissed. Which test should the nurse expect the provider to order?

options.text: Sweat chloride test
Serum immunoglobulin levels
Stool culture for bacteria
Barium swallow study

rationale.correct: A sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher supports a diagnosis of CF.

perOption.a: A high sweat chloride level confirms cystic fibrosis.
perOption.b: This tests for immune deficiency but does not explain the salty skin.
perOption.c: The stools suggest malabsorption, not infection.
perOption.d: This checks for aspiration but not for the salty skin or greasy stools.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old eating in a high chair suddenly cannot cry or cough and is turning blue but is still responsive. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give 5 back blows and then 5 chest thrusts, and repeat
Give 5 abdominal thrusts with the infant on the lap
Sweep a finger through the mouth to find and remove the object
Hold the infant upside down by the ankles and shake

rationale.correct: Infant choking: back blows and chest thrusts; start CPR if the infant becomes unresponsive.

perOption.a: This is the technique for infants under 1 year.
perOption.b: Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant's liver and organs.
perOption.c: A blind sweep can push the object deeper.
perOption.d: This is not recommended and can cause injury.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four children with pneumonia. Which finding should the nurse recognize as the earliest sign that a child's respiratory status is getting worse?

options.text: A 3-year-old, now restless, whose rate rose from 28 to 44/min
A 2-year-old with a heart rate that has fallen from 130 to 70/min
A 4-year-old with a blue tinge to the lips and lethargy
A 5-year-old with a cough producing yellow sputum

rationale.correct: Early: tachypnea, tachycardia, restlessness, retractions. Late: bradycardia, cyanosis, lethargy.

perOption.a: Rising respiratory rate and restlessness appear early as the child compensates for hypoxia.
perOption.b: Bradycardia is a late, ominous sign of hypoxia and impending arrest.
perOption.c: Cyanosis and lethargy are late signs.
perOption.d: This is expected with pneumonia.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize early respiratory distress in children.

questions.stem: Six hours after a tonsillectomy, a 5-year-old is resting with eyes closed. The pulse has risen from 96 to 124/min, the blood pressure is unchanged and the child has a sore throat and a temperature of 37.6 °C (99.7 °F). Which other finding most strongly suggests bleeding?

options.text: Swallowing every minute or so while asleep
Bad breath when the child opens the mouth
Refusing to drink because the throat hurts
Dark brown emesis of old blood in the first hour

rationale.correct: Post-tonsillectomy bleeding: frequent swallowing, clearing the throat, rising pulse and vomiting bright red blood.

perOption.a: Children swallow blood that trickles down the throat; with a rising pulse this suggests hemorrhage.
perOption.b: Halitosis is common during healing.
perOption.c: Throat pain is expected; fluids are encouraged.
perOption.d: Old swallowed blood from surgery is expected early.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving discharge teaching to the parent of a 6-year-old after a tonsillectomy. Which statement by the parent needs correction?

options.text: "I'll give cool fluids and ice pops to soothe the throat."
"I'll let my child drink through a straw to make it easier."
"I'll skip red or brown drinks and foods for the next week or so."
"I'll give acetaminophen on a schedule for the pain."

rationale.correct: After tonsillectomy: no straws, no red fluids, soft cool foods and watch for bleeding.

perOption.a: This soothes the throat and keeps the child hydrated.
perOption.b: Straws can dislodge clots and cause bleeding.
perOption.c: Red fluids can look like blood in emesis.
perOption.d: This is appropriate.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old has had four ear infections in 6 months. The parent formula-feeds and a grandparent who smokes provides daycare. After teaching, which parent statement shows understanding of how to prevent ear infections?

options.text: "I'll hold my baby semi-upright for every bottle."
"I'll give a bottle at bedtime so my baby sleeps longer."
"It's fine if Grandma smokes, as long as it's outside."
"I'll give a pacifier all day to help the ears drain."

rationale.correct: Reduce otitis media with upright feeding, breastfeeding, no smoke exposure and vaccines.

perOption.a: Feeding while lying flat lets fluid enter the short, horizontal eustachian tubes.
perOption.b: This increases ear infections and tooth decay.
perOption.c: Thirdhand smoke on clothes still increases risk.
perOption.d: Frequent pacifier use may increase risk.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old had tympanostomy tubes placed this morning for recurrent otitis media with effusion. The parent asks about care at home. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Use earplugs for swimming or baths if the provider advises
Clean inside the ears with cotton swabs each day
Pull the tubes out at home if they seem loose
Expect the tubes to stay in place for many years before removal

rationale.correct: Tympanostomy tubes: protect the ears from water per provider instructions and report drainage.

perOption.a: Water entering through the tubes can cause infection in some children.
perOption.b: Swabs can push wax in and damage the tubes.
perOption.c: Tubes are removed by the provider or fall out on their own.
perOption.d: They usually fall out on their own in 6 to 18 months.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the vital signs of four infants. Which set of findings is within the normal range for a 6-month-old who is awake and calm?

options.text: Heart rate 130/min, respiratory rate 40/min
Heart rate 80/min, respiratory rate 18/min
Heart rate 190/min, respiratory rate 72/min
Heart rate 95/min, respiratory rate 24/min

rationale.correct: Pediatric vital signs change with age; know the normal infant ranges.

perOption.a: Infants normally have a heart rate of about 100 to 160 and a respiratory rate of about 30 to 60.
perOption.b: These are adult values and are too low for an infant.
perOption.c: These are tachycardia and tachypnea.
perOption.d: These are below the infant range.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent of a 2-year-old with otitis media is going home with amoxicillin suspension 5 mL twice daily. The parent says, "I'll just use a teaspoon from the kitchen." How should the nurse teach the parent to measure the medicine?

options.text: With an oral syringe marked in mL
With a kitchen teaspoon filled to the brim
Mixed into a full bottle of milk or juice
With a dosing cup from another medicine

rationale.correct: Pediatric medications: give with an accurate oral syringe, directed into the side of the cheek.

perOption.a: Household spoons vary in size and give inaccurate doses.
perOption.b: Spoons vary in size.
perOption.c: The child may not finish the bottle.
perOption.d: Cups vary and may be marked differently.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old admitted 2 days ago with pneumonia screams, kicks and clings to the parent each time the parent leaves, and cries until falling asleep. The parent asks whether it would be better to stop visiting. What does the nurse recognize in this behavior?

options.text: The protest stage of separation anxiety, which is expected
Detachment, which shows the toddler is adjusting well
A sign of regression from a developmental delay
Despair, which means the visits are upsetting the child too much

rationale.correct: Separation anxiety stages: protest, despair, detachment. Encourage parents to stay and keep routines.

perOption.a: Protest is the first stage of separation anxiety in toddlers; continued visits help.
perOption.b: Detachment is the late stage, with apparent disinterest, and is not healthy adjustment.
perOption.c: This behavior is age-appropriate.
perOption.d: Despair is the quiet, withdrawn stage that follows protest.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old is 4 hours after surgery for a hernia repair. The toddler is restless, kicking, crying and hard to console. Which tool should the nurse use to assess the toddler's pain?

options.text: FLACC scale
Numeric 0 to 10 rating scale
Wong-Baker FACES scale
The parent's rating of the pain from 0 to 10

rationale.correct: Choose the pain scale by developmental level.

perOption.a: FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) suits preverbal children.
perOption.b: This is for school-age children and adults.
perOption.c: This is for children about 3 and older.
perOption.d: Parent input helps, but a validated observational tool is used.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent says their 7-month-old, who used to go to anyone, now cries and turns away when held by an aunt or the neighbor. The baby is otherwise meeting milestones. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Stranger anxiety is a normal stage at this age."
"This may be an early sign of a developmental problem."
"Your baby may have had a bad experience with them."
"Keep your baby away from visitors for a few months."

rationale.correct: Stranger anxiety appears around 6 to 8 months and is a sign of attachment.

perOption.a: Stranger anxiety usually starts around 6 to 8 months and shows healthy attachment.
perOption.b: It is a normal milestone.
perOption.c: This is unfounded.
perOption.d: This is not needed.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At a 2-year well-child visit, the nurse asks the parent about the child's speech. Which finding would the nurse expect for a typically developing 2-year-old?

options.text: Uses two-word phrases such as "more milk"
Speaks in sentences of 5 to 6 words
Says "mama" and "dada" but no other words
Can name and point to 4 colors

rationale.correct: Language milestones: first words around 12 months, two-word phrases at 2 years, simple sentences at 3.

perOption.a: Two-word phrases and about 50 words are typical at 2 years.
perOption.b: This is typical of a 4-year-old.
perOption.c: This is a delay at 2 years and needs evaluation.
perOption.d: Naming colors is typical around 3 to 4 years.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the parent of a 6-month-old who is breastfed about starting solid foods. Which statement by the parent shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll start with iron-fortified cereal or pureed meat."
"I'll stir a little honey into the cereal for flavor."
"I'll introduce one new food every 3 to 5 days."
"I'll keep breastfeeding along with the solids."

rationale.correct: No honey before 12 months; introduce single foods; no cow's milk as the main drink before 12 months.

perOption.a: Iron-rich foods are recommended around 6 months.
perOption.b: Honey can cause infant botulism before age 1.
perOption.c: This helps spot food allergies.
perOption.d: Breastfeeding continues.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 15 kg child admitted with dehydration is to receive maintenance IV fluids calculated by the Holliday-Segar method (100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg, plus 50 mL/kg for each kg from 11 to 20). What is the child's daily maintenance fluid requirement?

rationale.correct: First 10 kg: 10 × 100 = 1,000 mL. Next 5 kg: 5 × 50 = 250 mL. Total = 1,250 mL/day.
